text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you have a neck swelling; can you tell me how long you have noticed it and if it has changed in size? Is the area painful to the touch or does it hurt when you swallow?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Neck (Second Primary) with Metastasis to Cervical Lymph Nodes.

*Reasoning:* The patient presents with a painless, progressively increasing neck mass on the nape of the neck over two months, lacking fever or pain. This clinical picture is highly suspicious for a metastatic lymph node, specifically squamous cell carcinoma, given his age and location. The history of colon cancer (colectomy) could be a distractor or a separate history, but the specific "nape" location and painless, growing nature strongly point to a second primary head and neck malignancy rather than a recurrence of colon cancer, which would more likely present as a liver or lung metastasis or a distant node. The absence of fever and pain makes an acute infectious process (like an abscess) or a rapidly growing aggressive lymphoma less likely than a slow-growing carcinoma. The next step is to confirm
